newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan IV food makers say briefed doctors on saftey.
newsitem.headline: Japan IV food makers say briefed doctors on saftey.

text.p: Japanese makers of intravenous food supplements said on Tuesday that the products were safe when administered properly, adding that they would comply with an order to supply full instructions on their use to doctors.

Japan's Ministry of Health and Welfare issued an emergency order to the companies on Monday to provide full safety instructions on the use of the supplements which it said in a report were suspected of causing death in 41 cases since 1990.

Two of the eight companies which make the products, Terumo Corp and Tanabe Seiyaku Co Ltd, said that they would provide the information as requested, but added that they had supplied comprehensive guidance in the past on the safe use of the supplements.

"The problem was not with our products themselves, but with procedures under which the supplements were given to patients," said a Terumo spokeswoman. The spokeswoman said the company had provided doctors with information about how to use the products safely.
She added that the company does not expect the ministry's report to have a negative impact on its sales.

The ministry said it was looking into the exact cause of death in the 41 cases. A ministry spokesman said complications including unconsciousness, low blood pressure and memory failure may occur when the high-calorie food supplements are given to patients whose bodies lack sufficient levels of vitamin B1.
"We cannot deny that the 41 deaths were due to the use of the food supplement but we are investigating the exact cause of death in all these cases," the spokesman said on Tuesday.
The ministry's order, repeating a previous directive, requires the companies to provide health professionals with detailed guidance on the correct use of the high-calorie food supplements.
A Tanabe spokesman said that the supplements need to be used with Vitamin B1 to avoid possible side effects and the company had repeatedly stressed this point with hospitals and doctors.
Tanabe will provide doctors with a fresh version of detailed information on how to use the supplements, the spokesman said.
The ministry said some 40,000 to 50,000 people in Japan receive such high-calorie supplements every day, accounting for annual sales of 38 billion yen.
Shares in Terumo fell 30 at 2130 yen at midday, while Tanabe shares were down 20 to 1040 yen.
